title: Nzinga Refuses to Sit on the Floor
text:
In 1622 the kingdom of Ndongo, in what is now Angola, was being ravaged by Portuguese troops and their allies from the colony at Luanda. Its king, Ngola Mbandi, sent his sister Nzinga to Luanda to negotiate peace with the new Portuguese governor, Joao Correia de Sousa.

The Capuchin missionary Antonio Cavazzi, who later knew Nzinga, recorded what tradition said happened at the audience. When Nzinga entered, she found that the governor sat on a chair, while for her there was only a mat or cushion on the floor, the position of a subject. Nzinga did not protest. She signaled to one of her attendants, who knelt on all fours, and Nzinga sat on the woman's back for the whole meeting, level with the governor.

She then negotiated as an equal. She argued that Ndongo was a sovereign kingdom, not a conquered people, and that an ally was worth more to Portugal than a subject. She reached a peace agreement that included the removal of a Portuguese fort built on Ndongo land. While in Luanda she was baptized, taking the name Ana de Sousa. The Portuguese did not keep the treaty, but Nzinga went on to rule Ndongo and Matamba and resisted Portugal for decades.
lesson: The setting of a negotiation often defines the roles before anyone speaks. Refuse a position that makes you smaller, calmly, before the talking starts.
people: Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba, Joao Correia de Sousa, Ngola Mbandi
source: Giovanni Antonio Cavazzi da Montecuccolo, Istorica descrizione de' tre regni Congo, Matamba et Angola (1687); Linda Heywood, Njinga of Angola (2017)
caveat: The chair episode is known from later accounts and may have been embellished.
